slides.title: The experience
say: Hi friends, welcome back.
Imagine you already designed a checklist for what counts as a valid partition.
Every piece is nonempty.
Every piece sits inside the original set.
The pieces cover everything and do not overlap.
Now a theorem gives you a new family of pieces.
You should not rewrite the checklist by hand.
You should reuse the definition and plug this family into it.

slides.title: The Turn wedge
say: Turn-Lang defines `Partition` once.
The laws live on the structure.
So when Judson 1.25 gives us `Classes`, the theorem does not copy those laws.
It says: build a `Partition<X>` using exactly this family.
slides.visualNotes: Briefly open `disjoint` and `cover` law bodies.

slides.title: Math receipt
say: Here is the receipt in the theorem statement.
`exists Partition<X>[..Classes]` means: use this class family as the pieces of the partition.
The spread syntax is the bridge between data and reusable structure.
slides.screen:
```turn
theorem "equivalence classes form a partition (Judson Theorem 1.25 forward)" {
    forall X: Set<Any>,
    forall E: EquivalenceRelation<X>,
    exists Classes: Set<Set<Any>> where { ... },
    |- exists Partition<X>[..Classes]
}
```
slides.visualNotes: Highlight `[..Classes]` and link mentally to the structure definition.

slides.title: Close
say: So you define the laws once, spread the data, prove the obligations.
That is how the library stays maintainable.
slides.screen: Split screen: `Partition` laws on left, theorem conclusion on right.
slides.visualNotes: Short close.

slides.title: The experience
say: Hi friends, welcome back.
You have probably heard the slogan: invertible means bijective.
But a slogan is not a proof.
If I say a machine has an undo button, what evidence do I actually get?
I get a second machine that sends outputs back to inputs.
And I get two promises: doing, then undoing, gets you back; undoing, then doing, also gets you back.
That is the background you need before the formal proof makes sense.
slides.screen: Picture: A --f--> B and B --g--> A, with two round-trip arrows back to identity.
slides.visualNotes: Do not open the theorem yet. Make the inverse feel like an undo machine with two receipts.

slides.title: The Turn wedge
say: Turn-Lang makes the evidence inspectable.
The proof starts from the word invertible, unfolds it, and unpacks an inverse witness.
After that, the proof is not magic — it uses the composition equations carried by that witness.
slides.visualNotes: Collapse the backward direction for now. Highlight `unfold Function.invertible` and `witness gInv`.

slides.title: Math receipt
say: In the injective branch, two different inputs cannot land at the same output, because the inverse would send that same output back to two different places.
In the surjective branch, the preimage of b is simply gInv of b.
That is the proof idea hiding behind the slogan.
slides.screen:
```turn
split_conjunction {
    unfold Function.injective at goal
    assume hneq
    unfold Composition.def at hGf
    specialize hGf for x as a_1 into hLeft
    specialize hGf for x as a_2 into hRight
    ...
    contradiction hneq hRight
} {
    unfold Function.surjective at goal
    witness gInv.apply(b) for a
    exact hCover
}
```
slides.visualNotes: Do not read every line — point at `witness gInv for inv` and `contradiction`.

slides.title: Close
say: This is why Turn proofs are longer than slogans.
They show the evidence the slogan depends on.
Open the file, replay the proof, pause where you need.
slides.screen: Theorem name in tab + checkmark if proof complete.
slides.visualNotes: Encourage replay in workspace.

slides.title: Cartesian product
say: The book starts with the Cartesian product.
A times B is the set of ordered pairs — take one element from A, one from B, pair them up.
In Turn-Lang that is `CartesianProduct`.
The `for i in 1..n` block lists the factor sets A₁ through Aₙ.
`@notation(chain(...))` renders them as A₁ × A₂ × … in math.
For the binary case — a relation from A to B — note we can just use an array: `CartesianProduct<[A, B]>`, same structure, n equals two.
slides.visualNotes: Highlight `for i in 1..n`, `@notation(chain`, and `CartesianProduct<[A, B]>` callout.

slides.title: ℝⁿ waits for Tao

slides.title: Relations
say: Next, we have relations.
Think of a bag of ordered pairs — each pair picks something from A and something from B.
The book says that is a subset of A times B.
In Turn-Lang, `Relation` is itself a `Set` — and the `subset` law says every member of self must already be a pair in `CartesianProduct<[A, B]>`.
So the law is really a membership rule: nothing outside A × B can sneak in.
slides.visualNotes: Show math render of ⊆ A × B. Animate `[a b] in self` → pair in A × B.

slides.title: Functions as mappings
say: A function is not a separate species — it is a relation that behaves like a machine.
Feed in a, get exactly one b back; the pair [a b] is in the relation.
Turn-Lang puts the uniqueness check on `Relation` as `well_defined`, then `Function` refines `(well_defined)Relation`.
Instead of writing pairs by hand, we write f(a) — that is `apply` when you plug in a specific element a from the domain.
slides.visualNotes: Flash `sets-figure-mappings` — f is a mapping, g is not. Highlight `apply(a: domain)`.

slides.title: Well-defined
say: The book’s classic trap is f(p/q) equals p on rationals.
One half and two fourths are the same input, but the rule would output 1 and 2 — two different answers for one number.
That is what “not well-defined” means in plain language: one input, more than one output.
Our `well_defined` property formalizes exactly that — for each a, exists unique b with [a b] in the relation.
We do not need polynomial syntax in this video; the property already carries the intuition.
slides.screen: `well_defined` block on `Relation`. Cross out f(p/q) paragraph in XML.
slides.visualNotes: Side-by-side: ambiguous outputs vs unique b.

slides.title: Onto, one-to-one, bijective
say: Next the book defines onto, one-to-one, and bijective maps.
In Turn-Lang these live in a `properties` block on `Function` — adjectives you can attach to a map, not the `Subset` relation from video 1.1.
Surjective: for every b in the range, some a maps to it — forall b, then exists a.
Injective: distinct inputs give distinct outputs.
Bijective bundles surjective and injective.
The `domain_def` law says apply(a) always lands in the range.
slides.visualNotes: Pause on surjective quantifier order.

slides.title: Composition
say: The book defines composition next: f from A to B, g from B to C, and (g ∘ f)(x) equals g(f(x)).
Turn-Lang: structure `Composition` — when you `apply` on a specific x, you run f first, then g.
slides.visualNotes: Flash `sets-figure-composition` from XML.

slides.title: Three laws — one job each
say: Mark which pairs belong together.
Reflexive: everything groups with itself.
Symmetric: grouping cannot run one way only.
Transitive: grouping cannot fork through a middleman.

slides.title: The experience
say: Hi friends, welcome back.
This is Turner.
Suppose I say every room in a hotel has a guest.
That does not mean every guest has their own room.
The order of “for every” and “there exists” changes the picture.

If that direction is wrong, you are not a little wrong.
You are proving a different statement.

slides.title: The trap
say: Hi friends, welcome back.
This is Turner.
Homework says: let g be the inverse of f, and prove something about g.
Sounds normal.
But what if f is not invertible?
On paper you might still write g and hope the grader looks away.
You are not stuck because you are bad at proofs.
You are stuck because the exercise smuggled in a false premise.
slides.screen: Homework line: “Let g be the inverse of f.” Under it, a map that fails invertibility (e.g. f(x)=x² on ℝ→ℝ) — one picture, no lecture.

slides.title: The honest move
say: The honest move is not to force a proof.
It is to name what the question assumed.
Invertible is not a vibe — it means an inverse actually exists with the right laws.
If f does not have one, every line after “let g” is built on air.
slides.screen: Short checklist: premise stated? → premise true? → only then prove.

It says there exists an inverse structure, and that structure has laws to check.
Try to use invertible on a map that does not qualify, and the checker will not let you treat the assumption as free.
That is the point: catch the bad premise before you “prove” nonsense.

slides.title: Parallel proofs at the same fork
say: Here is the idea.
At this fork I already have a default proof line.
When I add `#!`, I am plugging in another proof in parallel.
Same goal, different strategy — maybe `assume` and `split`, maybe `contradiction`.
I keep both in the file so I can compare them, fold the failed one, and move on.

It does not.
The trial is its own parallel proof from the same fork point.

slides.title: The experience
say: Hi friends, welcome back.
In the last clip, a relation was a table of allowed input-output pairs.
Now imagine the table is supposed to behave like a machine.
You put in one input, and the machine is not allowed to return two different outputs.
That single-valued rule is the whole jump from relation to function.
So the design question is: should Turn invent a brand-new object, or reuse the relation we already understand?
slides.screen: Pipeline sketch: one input → one output (no code yet).
slides.visualNotes: Show relation table turning into a one-output machine. Question before symbols.

slides.title: The Turn wedge
say: Turn-Lang puts single-valuedness on `Relation` as a named property — for each input, a unique output in the relation.
Then `Function` refines that relation and adds `apply` — one inheritance line you can read on screen.
slides.screen:
`well_defined` on `Relation`, then:

```turn
structure Function<domain range: Set<Any>>: (well_defined)Relation<domain, range> {
    @notation( {self} ~ "(" ~ {a} ~ ")" )
    apply(a: domain): range,
```

Click Relation → Function in outline.
